questions.prompt: What does the `_ALL` suffix on an Oracle Fusion Financials table name, such as `AP_INVOICES_ALL`, actually indicate?
options: The table stores rows across every business unit or operating context at once, not just one
The table has been fully migrated from Oracle E-Business Suite terminology
Every column in the table allows NULL values
The table is read-only and can never be updated by a transaction
The table only exists in the production environment, not in test or practice instances
The table stores archived data going back across every fiscal year, not just the current one
questions.explain: The `_ALL` suffix is a holdover from Oracle's multi-org architecture: it means the table spans every business unit or operating context at once. Forgetting to filter or join an `_ALL` table by business unit is exactly the 'multi-org bleed' mistake the course warns about — rows from unrelated parts of the business silently combine into one result, with no error raised.
questions.distractorExplain: Option F reads 'ALL' as 'all time' — every fiscal year ever recorded — which is a natural but wrong guess. The suffix has nothing to do with history or archiving; `AP_INVOICES_ALL` holds the current, live set of invoices across every business unit, not a multi-year archive. Scope is the axis `_ALL` describes, not time.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about business units and ledgers, per lesson 2.
options: A business unit is the operational boundary a transaction is processed under, typically carried on transaction tables as BUSINESS_UNIT_ID
A ledger is defined by chart of accounts, calendar, currency, and convention — the 'four Cs'
A business unit and a ledger must always correspond one-to-one
Multiple business units can all post their accounting into the same ledger
Data access sets secure which ledgers a user can view inside General Ledger, separate from business-unit transactional security
questions.explain: A business unit is the operational boundary (BUSINESS_UNIT_ID); a ledger is the accounting boundary defined by the four Cs. Several business units can share one ledger, so the two don't have to match one-to-one — a single business unit is assigned one primary ledger, but a ledger can serve many business units. Data access sets are a separate security mechanism layered on top of ledgers inside GL, distinct from the business-unit security that governs subledger transactions.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Oracle Fusion Cloud's quarterly update code is a two-digit year followed by a ________ identifying the quarter.
questions.explain: Lesson 3 describes Oracle's quarterly release cycle as a two-digit year followed by a letter for the quarter. Documentation on docs.oracle.com is published per release, so a table reference page is tied to a specific quarter's version of the product — worth checking when something looks different between the docs and a practice environment.

questions.prompt: Match each table-name prefix to the module it identifies.
questions.explain: AP_ identifies Payables tables, AR_ identifies Receivables tables, XLA_ identifies the shared Subledger Accounting engine that every subledger routes through on its way to the General Ledger, and HZ_ identifies the Trading Community Architecture tables that hold shared party identity for suppliers, customers, and contacts alike.

questions.prompt: POZ_SUPPLIERS uses VENDOR_ID as its primary key column, even though the Fusion user interface always refers to 'supplier,' never 'vendor.' Why?
options: VENDOR_ID is a naming holdover from Oracle E-Business Suite terminology that Fusion kept for this key column
VENDOR_ID actually refers to the software vendor that licenses Oracle Fusion, not the supplier
POZ_SUPPLIERS is a temporary table name that will be renamed to use SUPPLIER_ID in a future release
VENDOR_ID is a computed column derived from PARTY_ID, not a true primary key
questions.explain: Lesson 5 is explicit about this: despite the Fusion UI always saying 'supplier,' the underlying `POZ_SUPPLIERS` table kept `VENDOR_ID` as its primary key column name as a holdover from Oracle E-Business Suite terminology. The supplier's displayed number lives in a `SEGMENT1` flexfield column on the same table, and its name comes from `HZ_PARTIES` through `PARTY_ID` — `VENDOR_ID` is simply the legacy key name, not a different concept.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about HZ_PARTIES and HZ_CUST_ACCOUNTS, per lesson 6.
options: HZ_PARTIES stores core identity with no financial data or credit terms attached
A single party can have more than one customer account
HZ_CUST_ACCOUNTS is the same table as HZ_PARTIES, just filtered down to rows that happen to be customers
Each customer account carries its own account number and its own credit and payment terms
HZ_CUST_SITE_USES_ALL records the business purpose of a site, such as bill-to or ship-to
questions.explain: HZ_PARTIES is deliberately party-centric: it records that an entity exists, with no business relationship attached. The actual customer relationship — credit terms, payment terms, account number — is recorded separately in HZ_CUST_ACCOUNTS, and one party can have more than one such account (a person's personal account and their business's account, for example). HZ_CUST_SITE_USES_ALL then layers the business purpose, like bill-to or ship-to, on top of a customer account's sites. HZ_CUST_ACCOUNTS is a genuinely different table from HZ_PARTIES, not a filtered view of it — both rows exist, linked by PARTY_ID.

questions.prompt: Match each table to what it actually stores.
right: The business purpose of a customer site, such as bill-to or ship-to
A raw address — street, city, state, postal code — independent of any party
Purchasing/payment-specific flags like pay-site and purchasing-site
A specific party's use of a specific location
questions.explain: HZ_LOCATIONS holds the raw address, unattached to any party. HZ_PARTY_SITES connects a specific party to a specific location. Each product then layers its own attributes on top of that same party-site relationship: POZ_SUPPLIER_SITES_ALL_M adds pay-site/purchasing-site flags, while HZ_CUST_SITE_USES_ALL adds the business purpose (bill-to, ship-to) of a customer account's site.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: supplier bank account details are stored in Oracle Payments schema tables, prefixed ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 5 points to the `IBY_` prefix (most notably `IBY_EXT_BANK_ACCOUNTS`) as where supplier bank account details actually live — not directly on `POZ_SUPPLIERS`. These rows connect back to the relevant party, since bank and branch are themselves represented as parties in HZ_PARTIES.

questions.prompt: A single invoice line on a supplier invoice can be split across multiple cost centers. Which table actually records that split, and why isn't it just stored on the invoice line itself?
options: AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_ALL records the split, because a distribution is the actual accounting breakdown and one line can map to more than one of them
AP_INVOICE_LINES_ALL records the split directly, by allowing multiple ACCOUNT columns on a single row
GL_JE_LINES records the split, since it's the first table in the overall chain where accounting amounts appear
AP_PAYMENT_SCHEDULES_ALL records the split, since it tracks amounts owed per account
questions.explain: Lesson 8 draws this distinction deliberately: an invoice line is not the same thing as an accounting distribution. A line's amount can be split across multiple accounts, and that split lives in AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_ALL, generated manually, from a distribution set, or automatically from a matched PO or receipt. It's the distribution rows, not the lines themselves, that feed Subledger Accounting on the way to the General Ledger.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the difference between an invoice being 'scheduled,' 'applied,' and 'disbursed,' per lesson 9.
options: AP_PAYMENT_SCHEDULES_ALL records a plan — due dates and amounts expected — that exists the moment an invoice is validated, whether or not money has moved yet
AP_INVOICE_PAYMENTS_ALL records a many-to-many relationship: one invoice can be paid across multiple payments, and one payment can cover multiple invoices
The actual check number or EFT reference is tracked directly inside AP_INVOICE_PAYMENTS_ALL
An invoice can be fully scheduled but not yet applied to any payment
Once a payment is applied in AP_INVOICE_PAYMENTS_ALL, disbursement is guaranteed to have already happened
questions.explain: A payment schedule is a plan that exists from the moment of validation, independent of whether money has moved. AP_INVOICE_PAYMENTS_ALL records the actual many-to-many linkage between invoices and payments. Scheduled, applied, and disbursed are three separate states — an invoice can be scheduled without being applied. The physical check or EFT reference, though, lives in Oracle Payments (the IBY_ tables), not in AP_INVOICE_PAYMENTS_ALL, and being applied doesn't guarantee disbursement has already completed.

questions.prompt: Match each Receivables table to what it actually represents.
right: The authoritative remaining balance owed on a transaction
The header for Receivables transactions, covering invoices, credit memos, and more
The matching of a receipt to one or more transactions
The receipt itself — money that came in, not yet matched to anything
questions.explain: RA_CUSTOMER_TRX_ALL is the transaction header, covering invoices, debit memos, credit memos, and more in one structure. AR_PAYMENT_SCHEDULES_ALL carries the authoritative open balance, updated whenever activity occurs. AR_CASH_RECEIPTS_ALL records the receipt itself. AR_RECEIVABLE_APPLICATIONS_ALL records how a receipt gets matched against one or more transactions, with statuses from applied to unidentified.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in AR_RECEIVABLE_APPLICATIONS_ALL, a status of ________ means the cash has come in but hasn't yet been matched to any transaction.
questions.explain: Lesson 10 lists the status values on AR_RECEIVABLE_APPLICATIONS_ALL: APP (applied), UNAPP (unapplied — cash came in but isn't matched to a transaction yet), ACC (on-account), and UNID (unidentified, meaning Oracle doesn't even know which customer the money belongs to).

questions.prompt: Put these stages of a supplier invoice's lifecycle in the order they occur, per lesson 12.
items: The invoice is validated (checked for completeness and matched against a PO if required)
The invoice is accounted (a subledger journal entry is generated)
The invoice's accounting is posted to the General Ledger
The invoice is scheduled for payment
questions.explain: Lesson 12 walks through exactly this sequence: entered, then validated, then accounted, then posted to GL, then scheduled for payment, then actually paid. Each stage leaves evidence somewhere in the data model, but no single column summarizes the whole lifecycle — which is exactly why reading only one status column (like the AP header status) can't answer 'is this paid.'

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of the `GL_BALANCES` table in Oracle Fusion's General Ledger?
options: It stores pre-summarized actual, budget, and encumbrance balances by code combination, period, and currency, so reports don't have to re-aggregate every journal line
It stores the individual debit and credit lines of every journal entry ever posted
It stores the chart of accounts, calendar, currency, and convention that define a ledger
It stores the open, unapplied amount remaining on every customer transaction
It stores which business units are permitted to post into a given ledger
It stores the raw subledger transaction before it has been accounted
questions.explain: Lesson 14 explains that technically a report could sum every GL_JE_LINES row to get a balance, but at real scale that's slow — so Oracle Fusion maintains GL_BALANCES as a table of pre-summarized actual, budget, and encumbrance balances by code combination, period, and currency. Most financial reports, including OTBI subject areas, query GL_BALANCES directly rather than re-aggregating every journal line on demand.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes GL_JE_LINES, not GL_BALANCES — GL_JE_LINES is exactly where the individual debit/credit lines of a posted journal entry live, each pointing to a CODE_COMBINATION_ID. GL_BALANCES is a separate, pre-summarized layer built on top of those lines specifically so reports don't have to re-aggregate them every time, which is the whole reason the two tables exist as distinct things.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of one supplier invoice's journey from Payables into a reported General Ledger balance in the correct order, per lesson 15.
items: The invoice and its distributions are recorded in AP_INVOICES_ALL / AP_INVOICE_LINES_ALL / AP_INVOICE_DISTRIBUTIONS_ALL
XLA_TRANSACTION_ENTITIES identifies the transaction generically, and XLA_EVENTS records the accounting event
XLA_AE_HEADERS and XLA_AE_LINES record the subledger journal entry itself, linked back to the source distribution through XLA_DISTRIBUTION_LINKS
GL_IMPORT_REFERENCES bridges the subledger journal entry into the General Ledger
GL_JE_HEADERS and GL_JE_LINES record the posted journal entry, which rolls up into GL_BALANCES
questions.explain: Lesson 15 traces exactly this chain: the Payables source tables, then Subledger Accounting's generic transaction/event layer, then the subledger journal entry itself (linked back to its source distribution via XLA_DISTRIBUTION_LINKS), then the GL_IMPORT_REFERENCES bridge, and finally the posted GL journal entry, which rolls up into GL_BALANCES. The same chain applies to any subledger — only the starting tables change.

questions.prompt: Match each General Ledger or Subledger Accounting table to what it actually stores.
right: Ties a subledger journal line back to the specific source distribution that caused it
A named group of one or more journal entries entered or imported together
One row per journal entry, including JE_SOURCE and PERIOD_NAME
The actual debit/credit amounts, each pointing to a CODE_COMBINATION_ID
questions.explain: GL_JE_BATCHES groups one or more journal headers together. GL_JE_HEADERS stores one row per journal entry, including JE_SOURCE (where it came from) and PERIOD_NAME. GL_JE_LINES stores the actual debit/credit amounts, each tied to a CODE_COMBINATION_ID. XLA_DISTRIBUTION_LINKS is the precise tie between a subledger journal line and the source distribution row that produced it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about GL_PERIODS and the ENTERED/ACCOUNTED columns on GL_JE_LINES, per Chapter 4.
options: A period with status Permanently Closed cannot be reopened, even for a genuinely necessary correction
A period with status Future Enterable allows journals to be entered in advance, even though it isn't yet open for normal posting
ENTERED_DR/ENTERED_CR and ACCOUNTED_DR/ACCOUNTED_CR always hold identical amounts, regardless of currency
A period with status Closed can, in principle, still be reopened if genuinely necessary
GL_PERIODS stores pre-summarized balances by period, the same role GL_BALANCES plays
questions.explain: Permanently Closed is exactly that — no further activity, full stop, unlike Closed, which could still be reopened if genuinely necessary. Future Enterable lets journals be entered ahead of a period opening for normal posting. ENTERED and ACCOUNTED amounts only match when a transaction is already in the ledger's own functional currency; for a foreign-currency transaction, the two pairs of columns differ, which is exactly why mixing them when summing produces a quietly wrong total. GL_PERIODS defines period names, date ranges, and status — it isn't where balances are pre-summarized; that's GL_BALANCES.

questions.prompt: Lesson 17 recommends starting a personal data map from a real business question, such as 'which suppliers have invoices open longer than 30 days,' rather than an abstract table list. Why?
options: Starting from a question forces you to identify a driving table and trace outward only as far as the question requires, so you learn tables attached to a reason you'll remember
Oracle's documentation only covers tables that are referenced inside a specific business question
A table-list approach is technically impossible, because Oracle doesn't publish a list of its own tables
Business questions are the only way to gain access to OTBI subject areas
questions.explain: Lesson 17 is explicit that trying to memorize 'all the AP tables' as an abstract exercise rarely sticks. Starting from a real business question forces you to identify a driving table and trace outward only as far as the question requires, so tables get learned in the order you'll actually need them, attached to a reason you'll remember — not as an arbitrary list.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the recurring data problems covered in the final lesson of this course.
options: Duplicate party records happen because HZ_PARTIES is entered by people, not generated programmatically
A stuck transaction typically shows as an XLA_EVENTS row with no corresponding XLA_AE_HEADERS row
Summing ENTERED amounts across transactions in different currencies produces a result that errors out immediately
Multi-org bleed happens when a query against an _ALL table forgets to filter or join by business unit
AR_PAYMENT_SCHEDULES_ALL.STATUS reading OPEN always means a materially significant balance remains
questions.explain: Duplicate parties are a human-data-entry problem, since HZ_PARTIES isn't generated programmatically. A stuck transaction is visible as an XLA_EVENTS row with no matching XLA_AE_HEADERS row, pointing to a configuration gap in the accounting rules. Multi-org bleed is exactly the _ALL-table mistake of forgetting to filter by business unit. Mixing ENTERED amounts across currencies doesn't error — it runs fine and returns a plausible-looking but meaningless total, which is precisely what makes it dangerous. And STATUS = OPEN can coexist with a negligible remaining balance (a rounding leftover), which is why the numeric amount, not the status word, is the authoritative signal.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a transaction that has an XLA_EVENTS row but no corresponding ________ row usually means something in the configured accounting rules didn't match that transaction's specific attributes.
questions.explain: The final lesson describes a 'stuck transaction' as one that's been validated but never actually accounted — visible as an XLA_EVENTS row with no corresponding XLA_AE_HEADERS row. This isn't a performance issue; it's a configuration gap, and it's exactly why the end-to-end trace from lesson 15 is a genuinely useful diagnostic skill rather than just an academic exercise.
